title: Peak Elevation Lookup: Summit Heights
description: Look up the elevation of peaks and ridgelines with the Peak Elevation Lookup — terrain data for summits worldwide, in feet and metres. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, clicking Everest returns the neighbourhood of 8,849 m — the terrain model's grid slightly softens knife-edge summits, while the surveyed figure stands at 8,848.86 m.
quick_answer: The Peak Elevation Lookup reads the elevation of mountain peaks and ridgelines from global terrain data: click a summit and get its height in feet and metres. Use it to check the peak across the valley, settle which of two summits is higher, and put numbers on the skyline.

examples.label: Example · The model versus the survey

body.t: Global terrain grids sample every ~30 m and average cells; a sharp summit's cell includes its shoulders, so model readings on pointy peaks run slightly low. Everest's cell will not read the full 8,848.86 m — the survey's theodolite-and-GNSS figure is the record; the model is the scout.
A 1,345 m Ben Nevis dominates its skyline more than a 3,000 m shoulder of a giant does — height is absolute, presence is relative. The lookup gives the absolute number; the eye reports the rest.

faq: Why does the summit read lower than the book value?
Grid averaging: the model's cell containing the summit also contains descending ground. The sharper the peak, the larger the shave — a known, bounded effect of ~30 m data.
Yes — any clicked point reads the terrain height there, so the col between two peaks (the number that defines prominence) is one click away.
The terrain model's ocean is sea level; seamounts need bathymetry this dataset does not carry. Land peaks only, honestly stated.
Eruptions rewrite summits (St Helens lost 400 m in 1980). The model reflects its survey era; recently remodelled volcanoes may disagree with it — news beats data there.
Both shown together, converted exactly (1 ft = 0.3048 m).
The Seven Summits shelf: Everest, Aconcagua (6,961 m), Denali, Kilimanjaro, Elbrus (5,642 m), Vinson (4,892 m), and Puncak Jaya or Kosciuszko depending on the list's continent convention.
Can I trust it for a first ascent claim?
No — first-ascent and record claims live on surveyed GNSS measurements. This page is for research, captions and curiosity, and says so.
The lookup reads terrain at your click rather than a gazetteer — an unnamed summit still gets its height, which gazetteers cannot offer.
